message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give a written notice of intent to stay.
• The deposit can only be used for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear & tear, or cleaning if the lease specifies it. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection checklist.
• Take photos or videos of the unit before you move in and after you move out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep a copy.
• If the issue is serious (e.g., mold, pest infestation, broken heating), you can withhold rent or seek a court order for repairs. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: you must follow the lease’s termination clause. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Terms** | • The lease must be in writing if it lasts longer than one year.
• The lease can’t contain illegal clauses (e.g., waiving your right to a habitable home). | • Read the lease carefully before signing. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights group or attorney. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (e.g., give notice, keep receipts). | • Keep receipts and document the problem. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or disturbances in writing. | | **Subletting** | • The lease may allow or prohibit subletting. If allowed, you usually need the landlord’s written consent. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the systems. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renters’ insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Consider renters’ insurance to cover personal property and liability. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read the Lease** – Understand all terms, including rent amount, due date, late fees, maintenance responsibilities, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you if disputes arise. 3. **Know Your Rights** – Familiarize yourself with the above table and local tenant‑rights resources. 4. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, use email or certified mail to keep a record. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you face a problem (maintenance, harassment, potential eviction), contact a local tenant‑rights organization or legal aid before it escalates. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Information on landlord‑tenant laws, dispute resolution. | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | File discrimination complaints. | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | Fair Housing Act enforcement. | | **Local Legal Aid Societies** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | | **Tenant‑Rights Groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union)** | Advocacy, workshops, and legal referrals. | --- **Disclaimer:** This overview is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may alter how the law applies. If you have a particular issue or need personalized guidance, consider consulting a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
